A US court found Google to be a monopolist in general search services and general search text advertising because it violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act through exclusionary conduct [Source: ev-1]. Specifically, Judge Amit Mehta ruled on August 5, 2024, that Google’s practice of paying billions of dollars for default distribution deals—such as with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla—created a self-reinforcing loop where defaults generate scale, data, and quality that protect market dominance against rivals [Source: ev-1]. Evidence cited included CEO Sundar Pichai’s testimony that Google paid approximately $26.3 billion for distribution in 2021, and trial evidence showing Google paid Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue [Source: ev-1].

On August 5, 20 marking the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case of 2000 [Source: ev-1]. The court also ordered that Google may no longer pay for default search placement through revenue-sharing agreements and imposed limits on its acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1].
